newsitem.title: UK: U.S. pledges tough action on Bosnia war criminals.
newsitem.headline: U.S. pledges tough action on Bosnia war criminals.

text.p: The United States on Thursday pledged intensified efforts in pursuit of war criminals still at large in Bosnia one year after the Dayton peace accord ended 43 months of ethnic bloodletting.

U.S. Assistant Secretary of State and envoy to the former Yugoslavia, John Kornblum, also made clear Washington was happy to see increasing pressure from mass street protests on Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic.
Opposition supporters and students have marched in their thousands through Belgrade demanding Milosevic's resignation for alleged ballot-rigging in recent local elections.
Kornblum said that because the international community was making progress in the rebuilding of Bosnia after the war, Serbia's support was less essential than a year ago.
Asked by a BBC radio interviewer if the U.S. was unhappy to see Milosevic under pressure, Kornblum said: "Not at all."

Speaking on the final day of a major international conference on implementing Dayton, Kornblum said the 70 indicted war criminals still at large in Bosnia could expect renewed efforts to bring them before the Hague war crimes tribunal.
"We have been working on this throughout this year and we, in cooperation with others, are going to intensify our efforts," he said.
"There shouldn't be any assumption that because peace is being built and because a certain amount of normality has returned we are going to give up on the war crimes issue."
He made clear that the United States did not support any move to put the war criminals issue on the "back burner" in the interests of promoting peace and stability.
"We don't agree with that," he said.
Kornblum said the West had a strategy which included working more closely with the war crimes tribunal, intensified diplomatic cooperation and reinforcement of local police.

But he ruled out spectacular actions to arrest prominent indicted war crimals such as former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and his army chief Ratko Mladic, saying this might drive other war criminals underground.
"This has to be a broad approach, which includes the local police forces, and we are working very hard on that," Kornblum said.
Britain has appeared to take a more cautious approach to the war criminals question.
A British official said the investigatory capabilities of the war-crimes tribunal in the Hague should be boosted.
"The general objective is to enhance the intelligence flow," he said.
But he was careful to point out the risks of peacekeepers getting involved in any manhunt.
"It's all very well people talking about snatch squads, but what happens if it ends with six dead NATO soldiers?"

The London conference, attended by 50 national delegations, has focused on the restriction of freedom of movement across front lines, human rights violations and the issue of war criminals still on the loose.
The international war crimes tribunal for the former Yugoslavia in The Hague has indicted 75 people for crimes against humanity but has only five in jail.
The 50,000-strong NATO-led peace implementation force, due to be replaced later this month by a follow-up force half its size, has no mandate to hunt down war criminals.
